detailedFindings.sourceTitle: We normally use simple present tense to talk about countries and nationalities. Not only the verb to be can be useful to talk about this. Revise the following chart and check some examples.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: Even when we talk about this topic, the grammar rules must be respected.
To Be – works alone.
Other verbs – Use auxiliaries.
MOST COMMON QUESTIONS
- Where are you from?

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: Language Targets
sourceParagraphsOmitted: When we talk about countries and nationalities, there are three main aspects or functions we can cover.
All country names, nationalities and languages take CAPITAL LETTERS.

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about routines; also, the use of adverbs of frequency is common on this topic.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about routines; also, the use of adverbs of frequency is common on this topic.
1. Adverbs go before verbs since they modify them, EXCEPT for To Be.
She is always happy
2. NEVER has a negative connotation.
(no need for don’t/doesn’t)
They never visit me.
3. Adverbs can work in statements, negative sentences and questions.

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: Another common thing in English are the interrogative words which can be used in any tense. Check out the following examples and how to identify them.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: Another common thing in English are the interrogative words which can be used in any tense. Check out the following examples and how to identify them.
Peter sometimes goes to the beach on weekends by car because he loves it.
Every interrogative word asks for specific information; look at the chart:
Bonus: I normally go to class with Jane. Who do you normally go to class with?

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: Language Targets
sourceParagraphsOmitted: When we talk about daily routines there are three main aspects that we should take into account using the simple present tense.

The three aspects talk about the same function but they aim different targets in language. The second aspect, as seen in the example, uses mainly general or indefinite time expressions to differentiate itself from the third one.

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about jobs and occupations as we saw on the useful language before.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about jobs and occupations as we saw on the useful language before.
In the following chart you will see how this structure can be implemented.
Jake works in a bank.
Does he work in a bank?
I don’t work as a waiter / Do you work as a waiter?

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: 1. Most of the verbs take “-s” when using the third person rule. take – takes cook - cooks 2. Verbs that finish in “-sh”, “-ch”, “-s”, “-ss”, “-z”, “-x”, “-o”, receive “-es” when using the third person rule. 3. Verbs that finish in “-y” change to “-i” + “es” when using the third person rule.* play – plays* stay – stays*
sourceParagraphsOmitted: stop – stops
teach – teaches
copy – copies
*When the “y” is preceded by a vowel letter, just add “s” at the end of the verb.
When talking about Jobs and referring to an individual, we need to use the articles a – an (also called indefinite).
i.e. “John is an architect.”,
“Peter is a doctor.”
As you can see in the examples, ‘a’ is used before words that start with consonants and “an” before words that start with vowels.
go - goes

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: Language Targets
sourceParagraphsOmitted: Simple present tense helps us to talk about and describe jobs and occupations. In this chart you will see two main functions covered by this structure when talking about jobs.
We use verb TO BE to state what people are, as in the example provided.
We use other verbs to specify what people do.

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: TO CONSIDER - This / that (singular) These / Those (plural) are demonstratives we use to talk about possessions. This / These (close objects) – That / Those (far objects) - Whose: wh word used to ask for possessions: Whose USB is this? - Possessive adjectives can also be used to talk about belongings: This is my house. - Every possessive adjective has a possessive pronoun: My / Mine, Your / yours, His / His, Her / Hers, Its / Its, Our / Ours, Their / Theirs (used when we already know what we are talking about) - Demonstrative pronouns can also work as adjectives. E.G That house is blue. Let’s watch the video on the platform.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: - This / that (singular) These / Those (plural) are demonstratives we use to talk about possessions. This / These (close objects) – That / Those (far objects)
- Whose: wh word used to ask for possessions: Whose USB is this?
- Possessive adjectives can also be used to talk about belongings: This is my house.
- Every possessive adjective  has a possessive pronoun: My / Mine, Your / yours, His / His, Her / Hers, Its / Its, Our / Ours, Their / Theirs (used when we already know what we are talking about)
- Demonstrative pronouns can also work as adjectives. E.G That house is blue. Let’s watch the video on the platform.

sourceParagraphsOmitted: We normally use simple present tense to talk about places and where they are.
- Prepositions are used to indicate location.
- Downtown does not use any preposition: I am going downtown.
- More than 1 verb can be used to talk about directions. / Questions vary too.

sourceParagraphsOmitted: When we talk about places, we can consider the following aspects.
Prepositions are essential to work with these 3 aspects since they state locations and placement.

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: We normally talk about places and we include the use of adjectives to describe their characteristics. Adjectives are words we use to denote specificities about people, places or situations.
sourceParagraphsOmitted: We normally talk about places and we include the use of adjectives to describe their characteristics. Adjectives are words we use to denote specificities about people, places or situations.
Adjectives come before the object, place or people they describe.
They can also be after one verb:  My house is beautiful (mainly after To Be).
Adjectives do not change because of  gender. E.G: She is beautiful / The park is beautiful.
Adjectives are not pluralized. E.G: They are talls.❌ They are tall. ✅

detailedFindings.sourceTitle: Language Targets
sourceParagraphsOmitted: Adjectives can be used in any tense: present, past, future. They are mainly used to describe different characteristics. Check the following examples.
More than one adjective can be used to describe one single thing. It has to respect the order presented in the characteristics. E.G.
They have a gorgeous, big, new, American, wooden, beach house.
*not always all the characteristics are used*
